lens: Fact and integrity audit of /home/user/livewell-land/client/public/essays/did-the-resurrection-happen.json (updated 2026-10-28) against its claims ledger /home/user/livewell-land/docs/work/essays/ledgers/did-the-resurrection-happen.md, the BSB chapter files in /home/user/livewell-land/client/public/bible/ch/, the verifier's saved source copies in the session scratchpad (ESV 2011 from lguenth/mdbible; ANF Origen, Against Celsus book 2; ANF Justin, Dialogue; ANF 1 Clement; Gutenberg 9662 Hume Enquiry; Perseus Whiston Josephus and Perseus Tacitus; Sefaria export Mishneh Torah Kings), and the integrity rules in /home/user/Livewell-/docs/work/essays/BRIEF.md. Read-only. The published body differs from docs/work/essays/did-the-resurrection-happen.md only in dropping the title and standfirst lines and the two parenthetical links to essays that are not public. This run used 6 of its 30 web searches on 2026-10-28 and saw search-engine summaries only; it opened no page. Every Scripture quotation (33 strings) was re-compared by script with the ESV copy this run: all match. Every non-Scripture quotation was re-read in the saved primary text: all match word for word, but one Celsus quotation stops where Celsus's sentence goes on to the alternative he called most probable (finding 1).

findings.where: Could They Have Seen Visions?, first paragraph: 'In the same passage where Celsus mocked Mary Magdalene, he offered his own account of the appearances: the witness "had either dreamed so, owing to a peculiar state of mind, or under the influence of a wandering imagination had formed to himself an appearance according to his own wishes, which has been the case with numberless individuals."'
findings.problem: (c)/(d) The words match Origen, Against Celsus 2.55 (ANF), but the essay closes the quotation with a period at 'numberless individuals.' where Celsus's sentence runs on: '...which has been the case with numberless individuals; or, which is most probable, one who desired to impress others with this portent, and by such a falsehood to furnish an occasion to impostors like himself.' (re-read this run in the verifier's saved ANF copy, resv/pd/celsus2.txt). Celsus offered the dream or hallucination account as one of two and judged a deliberate falsehood the more probable. Calling the first 'his own account of the appearances' and stopping the quotation there tells the reader less than Celsus said, and the essay's later line that fraud 'has few defenders among scholars now' reads differently once you know Celsus favored it. The ledger line (Quotations of non-Scripture sources, second Celsus item) records the word match but not the cut.
findings.fix: Replace that sentence with: In the same passage where Celsus mocked Mary Magdalene, he offered his own account of the appearances. The witness "had either dreamed so, owing to a peculiar state of mind, or under the influence of a wandering imagination had formed to himself an appearance according to his own wishes, which has been the case with numberless individuals," or else, "which is most probable," had told a falsehood "to impress others with this portent." (Every quoted string is verbatim from Against Celsus 2.55, ANF.) Keep the next sentences as they are; 'The modern hallucination theory adds clinical vocabulary, but the idea is his' stays true. Add to the ledger line that the sentence continues with Celsus's 'most probable' alternative and that the essay now reports it.

findings.where: What Paul Handed On, third paragraph: 'Paul's visit to Jerusalem came a few years later, and the letter itself some twenty years after the crucifixion.'
findings.problem: (a) No ledger line dates the Jerusalem visit against the crucifixion. The ledger has only Galatians 1:18 ('after three years', counted from his conversion). A search this run (A. T. Robertson on ccel.org; Jamieson, Fausset and Brown on ccel.org; Arthur Just on ctsfw.edu, as summarized) gives estimates for Paul's conversion from AD 31 to 36 (JFB reports a spread to 42, most authorities 35 to 40) and the visit about three years later, so roughly AD 34 to 40. Against a crucifixion in 30 or 33 the gap runs from two or three years to about ten. 'A few years later' fits only the early chronologies.
findings.fix: Change to: Paul's visit to Jerusalem came within a decade, and the letter itself some twenty years after the crucifixion. (Or keep 'a few years later' only after a ledger line is added with a source that dates the visit within a few years of 30 or 33.)

findings.where: What Paul Handed On, third paragraph: 'Most scholars, including many with no stake in Christianity, think Paul received this summary within a few years of the events it describes.'
findings.problem: (c) The ledger's sources for this line (Pickup, JETS 2013; Lüdemann 1994 as reproduced; Carrier's site; Ehrman as quoted; the Wikipedia snapshot as summarized) speak of when the formula originated or was composed ('originated in the very earliest years of the Church', 'composed within a few years', 'the first two years after the crucifixion'), not of when Paul received it. The ledger line restates them as 'date Paul's reception of the summary', which is a step further than the sources it lists.
findings.fix: Change to: Most scholars, including many with no stake in Christianity, think this summary took shape within a few years of the events it describes.

findings.where: What Paul Handed On, second paragraph: 'Most of this list came to Paul already formed, and he passed it on as he got it.'
findings.problem: (a) No ledger line covers how much of the list is pre-Pauline. The sources in the ledger speak of 'a pre-Pauline confession, or creed, of some kind' and of 'the formula in 1 Corinthians 15:3-5'; verse 8 is Paul's own addition, and whether verses 6 and 7 belong to the received tradition is debated. 'Most of this list' is more precise than the sources.
findings.fix: Change to: The core of this list came to Paul already formed, and he passed it on as he got it.

findings.where: Was the Tomb Empty?, first paragraph: 'The strongest objection to that story comes from Ehrman.'
findings.problem: (a) No ledger line. 'Comes from' can be read as saying the argument originated with Ehrman, but the no-burial argument is older: John Dominic Crossan made it in Jesus: A Revolutionary Biography (1994), in the chapter 'The Dogs Beneath the Cross' (search this run: Ehrman's blog, ehrmanblog.org/?p=3090; Richard Beck's Substack notes; Kirkus Reviews, as summarized). 'The strongest' is the essay's own judgment, which is fine once the origin reading is removed.
findings.fix: Change to: Ehrman has pressed the strongest objection to that story.

findings.where: What "Resurrection" Meant, last paragraph: 'Rome killed him at Betar in 135.'
findings.problem: (c) The ledger supports Betar and 135 (McGiffert, Book 4 note 5: 'the place was taken in 135 a.d. ... and Bar-Cochba was put to death'; Britannica and Wikipedia as summarized). But the Maimonides passage the essay leans on (Kings and Wars 11:3, re-read this run) says only 'until he was killed because of sins', and the rabbinic sources give other accounts of how he died (from memory, not opened this run: Jerusalem Talmud Taanit 4:5 and Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 93b). 'Rome killed him' is the usual modern reading, but the plainer wording claims only what every source agrees on.
findings.fix: Change to: He died when Rome took Betar in 135.

findings.where: What Almost Every Historian Grants, second paragraph: 'So did James, a brother who had not believed in him during his ministry: "For not even his brothers believed in him" (John 7:5).'
findings.problem: (c) John 7:5 speaks of 'his brothers' as a group. James is named as one of them at Mark 6:3 (BSB checked this run), which the ledger does not cite. The essay hedges correctly later ('James, as far as the Gospels tell us, didn't believe in his brother while he lived') but states it flatly here, under a heading that claims near-agreement among historians.
findings.fix: Change to: So did James, one of the brothers who, John says, had not believed in him during his ministry: "For not even his brothers believed in him" (John 7:5). Add Mark 6:3 to the ledger line for James as Jesus' brother.

findings.problem: (c) The ledger lists three essay links, but the published JSON carries only /writing/the-historical-jesus (public: its JSON is landed and it is on the shelf). The other two were removed because those essays are not public (the-first-christians-died-for-this is 'pending' with no landed JSON; did-christianity-copy-pagan-myths is not on the shelf). The published text is right; the ledger is stale.
findings.fix: No essay change. Update the ledger Links line to say the published text keeps only /writing/the-historical-jesus and /help.

Hume: 'A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence' (§87) and 'should not have the least inclination to believe so miraculous an event' (§99) verbatim against Gutenberg 9662; the Queen Elizabeth details (first of January 1600, physicians and the whole court before and after her death, interred a month, resumed the throne, three years) match §99; 'has ever amounted to a probability' (§98) supports the paraphrase. 'Of Miracles', 1748: ledger line verified (EB1911).

Josephus: Jewish War 4.317 (crucified taken down and buried before sunset), Antiquities 4.219 (testimony of women not admitted), Antiquities 20.200 (James stoned) re-read in Perseus Whiston. Tacitus Annals 15.44 (Pilate; 'hated for their abominations') re-read in Perseus.

Maimonides, Kings and Wars 11:3: 'considered him to be the Messianic king until he was killed ... Once he was killed, they realized that he was not the Mashiach' re-read in the saved Sefaria export; paraphrase fair.

Numbers and dates with ledger lines and sources: mid-50s (corr. 26); 30 or 33 (corr. 27); some twenty years (corr. 28); Tacitus early 2nd century; 1968, Giv'at ha-Mivtar, Yehohanan, iron nail in the heel (corr. 25); Celsus late 2nd century; Justin mid-2nd century; Origen mid-3rd century; Rees 1971, BMJ, 293, almost half, normal and helpful (corr. 20); Wright some eight hundred pages (corr. 33); 132 and 135, Betar; Maimonides a thousand years later; James stoned around 62 (corr. 23); 1 Clement late 1st century; swoon theory two centuries ago (Paulus 1828); Hume 1748.

Craig Evans, 'Judea in peacetime': confirmed again by a search this run (logos.com/grow, 'How Ancient History Affirms the Resurrection of Jesus', as summarized: 'this Jewish custom was respected by the Romans, during peacetime', citing Philo and Josephus). A first search for the title found nothing; the exact-phrase search found it.

Dale Allison: a search this run (Catholic Answers; Philosophia Christi review page; Habermas critique listing, as summarized) supports the paraphrase that he gathers apparitions of the dead, including collective ones, and calls the apologists' many-witnesses rebuttal inadequate. Paraphrase only, no quotation marks.

Restoration (g): none outstanding. Every item under 'Original wording, for restoring' is already restored except 'one case among hundreds'. A search this run ('Ask Bart Ehrman Anything II' on Goodreads and Andrew Sullivan's Dish, as summarized) has Ehrman framing Yehohanan against 'thousands' of crucified victims, a figure he credits to other scholars; 'hundreds' is still not his figure, so the essay correctly keeps 'one case proves very little'.

Living persons: Ehrman (grants early belief; does not accept it was true; burial argument; visions in the bereavement sense; one case proves little), Evans, Allison (a Christian New Testament scholar) and Wright (historian, former Anglican bishop) are each described as their sources support, and none is caricatured. Borg (died 2015) is described as the ledger's sources support.
Biography: 'I was an atheist before I was a Christian' and 'Baptist churches like the one I pastor' match NOTES.md per the ledger; no title, years, book count, scene or convention.
